en: The *Śarīra-skandha-dhātv-āyatana-sūtra*, Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
The sūtras expounded by the Buddha and his instructions are all contained within three categories; these are combined here as one. What are they?
What are the three?
First, the five aggregates; second, the six bases; third, the spheres of entry.
What are the five aggregates?
First is form, second is feeling, third is perception, fourth is mental formations, and fifth is consciousness;
these are the five aggregates (*skandhas*).
The aggregate of form is called the ten manifest bases of form (*rūpāyatana*). What are these ten manifest bases of form?
First, the eye; second, visible forms; third, the ear; fourth, sounds; fifth, the nose; sixth, odors; seventh, the tongue; eighth, tastes; ninth, the body; tenth, tangibles.
These are the ten manifest bases of form (*rūpāyatana*).
This is called the category of form.
What is the category of sensation?
The category of sensation consists of the six sensations of the body:
First, the eye knows suffering; second, the ear knows suffering; third, the nose knows suffering; fourth, the tongue knows suffering; fifth, the body knows suffering; sixth, the mind knows suffering.
These are the six sufferings of the body, termed the "categories of suffering."
What are the types of perception?
There are six types of perception regarding the body:
first, perception of form; second, perception of sound; third, perception of odor; fourth, perception of taste; fifth, perception of tangibles; and sixth, perception of mental phenomena (*dharma*).
These are the six perceptions of the body, which are called the "perception-seed.
What is the "volitional-formation seed"?
The "contact-seed" refers to the six contacts of the body:
First, contact with forms; second, contact with sounds; third, contact with odors; fourth, contact with tastes; fifth, contact with tangibles; sixth, contact with mental phenomena (*dharma*).
These are the six contacts of the body, and these are called the categories of formations (*saṃskāra-varga*).
What are the seeds of consciousness?
The seeds of consciousness are called the six consciousnesses of the body:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
These are the six consciousnesses of the body; these are called the seeds of consciousness.
They are called the seeds of the five aggregates; one should know them as such.
From what is this known?
It is considered impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
From this, there are two kinds of knowledge:
first, the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñā-jñāna*), and second, the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
What is known through wisdom?
It is knowing that [all things] are impermanent, suffering, empty, and not-self; this is what is known through wisdom.
What is known through the knowledge of abandonment?
The severance of craving is known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the characteristic of the aggregates (*skandha*)?
Accumulation is the characteristic of the aggregates; sufficiency is the characteristic of the aggregates.

For example, a seed of matter is called a "seed of matter," a seed of wood is called a "seed of wood," a seed of fire is called a "seed of fire," and a seed of water is called a "seed of water"; all five aggregates are likewise so.
There are eighteen bases (āyatana). What are these eighteen bases?

First, the eye; second, forms; third, visual consciousness; fourth, the ear; fifth, sounds; sixth, auditory consciousness; seventh, the nose; eighth, odors; ninth, olfactory consciousness; tenth, the tongue; eleventh, tastes; twelfth, gustatory consciousness; thirteenth, the body; fourteenth, tangibles; fifteenth, tactile consciousness; sixteenth, the mind; seventeenth, mental phenomena (dharma); eighteenth, mental consciousness. These are called the eighteen bases.
Having already known this, from what is it known?
It is known by way of its impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; this constitutes knowing.
Furthermore, from this knowing there are two kinds of knowledge:
The first is knowledge through wisdom (*prajñā-jñāna*), and the second is knowledge through what has been abandoned (*prahīṇa-jñāna*).
What is knowledge through wisdom?
It is the realization that [phenomena] are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this is knowledge through wisdom.
What is knowledge through abandonment?
The abandonment of craving is knowledge through abandonment.
What is its fulfillment? What constitutes that fulfillment?
Some say there is no further completeness; since there is nothing further, it causes the eye to see clearly.
One who explains this has already severed the root of the eye and the root of the ear, and having explained it universally in this way, he is ultimately called a "Mūladhara" (Holder of the Root).
For example, as if a person were afflicted by much heat, such a term is "universal"; this analogy constitutes completeness.
There are also twelve bases (āyatana). What are these twelve?
There are six internal and six external. What are the six internal?
The first consists of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are the six internal bases (āyatana) of one's own person.
What are the six external ones?
They are visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; these constitute the twelve bases.
From what is all this known?
It is known from the fact that it is impermanent, suffering, empty, and not-self; furthermore, there are two ways of knowing:
first, knowing through wisdom (*prajñā*), and second, knowing through abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
What is known through the knowledge of wisdom?
It is knowing that [all things] are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this is what is known through the knowledge of wisdom.
What is known through the knowledge of abandonment?
The severance of craving is what is known as "knowledge through severance.
What is "entry"? Understanding that which leads to it is called entry; from entry comes understanding.

For example, because one enters through gold, it is called a "gold ground"; because one enters through silver, it is called a "silver ground. In this way, each should be understood according to its respective metaphor of that which is entered from and that which is entered into; such is existence arising from what is intended by the mind. In the same way, there are the practices of sinful and suffering dharmas arising from such mental intentions.
That which arises from this is called "entering from this.
There is also that which enters from this; for example, just as a king has the name "one who enters" his possessions, so it is with this as well.
There are four truths:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Suffering is called the essential; it refers to the body as well as mental formations.
Training is essential, and delusion is likewise what the world cherishes;
exhaustion is essential, and wisdom is likewise liberation;
the Path is essential, and tranquility is likewise insight.
There are also thirty-seven factors of the path (bodhipākṣika-dharmas):

the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path; these constitute the thirty-seven factors of the path.
The Buddhas of the past also had this; the Buddhas of the present also have this; the Buddhas of the future will also have this.
Pratyekabuddhas also attain the path that transcends the world through this, and the disciples of the Buddha likewise do so through this; this is the unconditioned path that transcends the world.
What are the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*)?

They are: a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body as body internally; he dwells contemplating the body as body externally; and he dwells contemplating the body as body both internally and externally. He applies his full attention to dispel worldly delusion and its unwholesome tendencies.
He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings internally; he dwells contemplating feelings as feelings externally; and he dwells contemplating feelings as feelings both internally and externally.
Exerting the full power of mental attention to dispel the world’s deluded mind and its discomfort:

one contemplates the internal mind with the mind and attains stillness; one contemplates the external mind with the mind and attains stillness; one contemplates both the internal and external mind with the mind and attains stillness—exerting the full power of mental attention to dispel the world’s deluded mind and its discomfort.

One contemplates internal phenomena with phenomena and attains stillness; one contemplates external phenomena with phenomena and attains stillness; one contemplates both internal and external phenomena with phenomena and attains stillness—exerting the full power of mental attention to dispel the world’s delusion and its discomfort.
What are the four right efforts?

First, when a corrupt and evil mental state has not yet arisen, a bhikṣu exerts himself to prevent its arising; he rouses his will and does not abandon his exertion, applies energy to restrain his mind, and abandons the distraction of evil thoughts—this is the first effort of the mind.

Second, when a corrupt and evil mental state has already arisen, he desires to sever it through pure dharmas; he rouses his will to seek the means, applies energy to restrain his mind, and abandons the distraction of evil thoughts—this is the second effort of the mind.

To encourage the mind to give rise to pure dharmas not yet arisen, employing skillful means to cause them to arise, exerting diligence to restrain the mind, and abandoning distracted or evil thoughts—these are the three [aspects of] the abandonment of mental states (*cittaprahāṇa*).

To cause pure dharmas already arisen to remain, not to be forgotten, not to diminish, and to increase—exerting diligence beyond mere increase to fully develop skillful means, and exerting diligence to restrain the mind and abandon distracted or evil thoughts—these are the four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
What are the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)?

There is a bhikṣu who, desiring to definitively sever birth and death, develops the basis of psychic power through concentration of desire; he detests attachment to birth and death, abandons the attachment of desire, and exhausts all attachment—this is the first basis of psychic power, the concentration of energy (*vīrya-samādhi*).

To sever birth and death, he develops the basis of psychic power through concentration of energy; he detests attachment to birth and death, abandons the attachment of desire, and exhausts all attachment; from this, he gives rise to a state of non-attachment and departs from it—this is the second basis of psychic power.

With concentration of mind, one cuts off birth and death; increasing the bases of psychic power through cultivation, one abandons attachment to the suffering of birth and death, removes attachment to desire, exhausts all attachments, and casts away that which arises from an unfavorable state of mind—this is the third base of psychic power.

With concentration of precept, one cuts off birth and death; increasing the bases of psychic power through cultivation, one abandons attachment to the suffering of birth and death, removes attachment to desire, exhausts all attachments, and casts away that which arises from an unfavorable state of mind—this is the fourth base of psychic power.
The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of power have already been fully explained.
What are the five faculties?
The faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom—these are called the five faculties.
In what sense are those faculties (indriya) "faculties"? What is the meaning of "faculty"?

Belonging [to a specific category] is the meaning of faculty; being desirable is the meaning of faculty; not acting for a common purpose is the meaning of faculty—this is called the meaning of "faculty."
What are the five powers?
They are the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom; these are called the five powers.
What is the meaning of those powers?

The meaning of power (*bala*) is that which cannot be destroyed; the meaning of power is that which is beneficial; the meaning of power is having courage; the meaning of power is being able to attain a basis—this is called the meaning of power.
There are seven factors of enlightenment. What are these seven factors of enlightenment? First, the factor of mindfulness;

second, the factor of investigation of phenomena; third, the factor of energy; fourth, the factor of rapture; fifth, the factor of tranquility; sixth, the factor of concentration; seventh, the factor of equanimity. These are called the seven factors of enlightenment.
There are eight factors of the path for those who have attained the Way.

What are these eight? First, right view; second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort; seventh, right mindfulness; eighth, right concentration.
These are called the eight factors of the path.
The eightfold path is condensed into three categories:
first, the category of ethical discipline (*śīla*); second, the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and third, the category of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Among these, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are termed the category of ethical discipline.
That which consists of right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration is called the seed of concentration;
that which consists of right view and right thought is called the seed of wisdom.
All follow these instructions, so that they may not only receive instruction, but also receive the intent of the instruction and the wisdom of the instruction.

Those bhikṣus who have cultivated the seeds of morality act to uproot the root of anger, to disperse the fetters of anger, to heal the wounds of anger, to recognize suffering, and to transcend the realm of desire.

That monk who is established in concentration acts to uproot the root of stinginess, to disperse the fetters of desire, to heal the wounds of desire, to understand the sensation of pleasure, and to transcend the realm of form.

That bhikṣu of wisdom-seed uproots the root of delusion, disperses the fetters of delusion, heals the wound of pride, knows neither the pain of dissatisfaction nor the pain of suffering, and attains transcendence beyond the realm of form.
These are the three kinds of bhikṣus:
those who dwell in order to uproot the three stains, disperse the three stains, heal the four sores, know the three pains, and cross over the three realms.

What are the twelve types? From seeking arises craving; from the causal condition of ignorance arises grasping; from grasping arises consciousness; from consciousness arise name-and-form; from name-and-form arise the six sense bases; from the six sense bases arises contact; from contact arise feelings; from feelings arises craving; from craving arises clinging; from clinging arises becoming; from becoming arises birth; and from birth arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and mental distress. Thus, this complete collection of the seeds of suffering constitutes the origin of suffering.

When ignorance (*avidyā*) is exhausted, mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted; when mental formations are exhausted, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is exhausted; when consciousness is exhausted, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is exhausted; when name-and-form is exhausted, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are exhausted; when the six sense bases are exhausted, contact (*sparśa*) is exhausted; when contact is exhausted, feeling (*vedanā*) is exhausted; when feeling is exhausted, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted; when craving is exhausted, grasping (*upādāna*) is exhausted; when grasping is exhausted, existence (*bhava*) is exhausted; when existence is exhausted, birth (*jāti*) is exhausted; when birth is exhausted, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are exhausted. When old age and death are exhausted, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are exhausted. In this way, the entire mass of suffering is brought to its end.

That delusion is defined as not knowing the Four Noble Truths as they truly are; it is failing to understand, failing to see, failing to correspond with, and failing to accept them; it is a lack of understanding and a failure to comprehend their fundamental roots—this is what is called delusion.
What are the six cravings that arise with ignorance as their cause?
They are the cravings for the six types of sensation. What are these six?
Forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are the six objects of the body that lead to feeling; these are called "grasping.
With grasping as a condition, there arise the six types of consciousness of the body: those of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the six consciousnesses of the body.

That consciousness has name-and-form as its causal condition. "Name" refers to the four non-material aggregates (skandhas), while "form" refers to the four great elements, namely earth, water, fire, and wind. "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness" constitute name.
Form constitutes the basis of the four great elements, which are earth, water, fire, and wind.
The former is "name" (nāma), and these four are "form" (rūpa); these two are interconnected and together constitute "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
Due to the conditions of that name-and-form, there arise the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) of the body:
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; this is called the experience of the six sense bases of the body.
With those six sense bases as condition, there arise the six types of mental intention regarding the body:
those of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the six types of mental intention regarding the body.
Conditioned by that craving, there arise the six types of bodily suffering:
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the six types of bodily suffering.
Conditioned by those sufferings, there arise the six types of attachment to the body.

Attachment to forms, attachment to sounds, attachment to odors, attachment to tastes, attachment to tangibles, and attachment to mental phenomena—these are called the six types of attachment to the body (*kāyatanhā*).
With that attachment as a condition, there arise four types of feeling (*vedanā*):

first, the feeling of sensual desire; second, the feeling of the fetter of views; third, the feeling of rules and observances; and fourth, the feeling of the fetter of "I am" (*asmimāna*)—these are called the four types of feeling.
With feeling as a condition, there is the formation of the three realms of existence:
first, the desire realm; second, the form realm; and third, the formless realm. These are called the three realms of existence.
That which arises through causes and conditions consists of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six bases (*āyatana*), and the six elements (*dhātu*).

When existence (*bhava*) is as it is, there is birth and accumulation; having passed away, one falls into the differentiation of the faculties (*indriya*), and having entered into the attainment of existence, this is called birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
What is meant by "what" and "whom"?
It refers to the person, wherever they are and wherever they go.
That which has already passed away and been destroyed, the time of death when life has ended and the faculties have ceased, this is called death.
The former is fundamentally old age, and the latter is ultimately death; therefore, it is called "old age and death.
What is the characteristic of delusion?
It is to see darkness within darkness.
If there is lack of understanding, it causes one to fall into the state of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).
What is the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*)?
That which causes there to be further existence hereafter is the characteristic of arising.
From this, one initiates [the process], causing one to fall from here into the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
What is the characteristic of consciousness?
It is the object of consciousness and the matter of consciousness; this is the characteristic of consciousness, which causes one to fall from here into the sphere of name-and-form (*nāmarūpasthiti*).
What is the characteristic of names?
It is their mutual dependence; this is the characteristic of names, which causes one to fall into the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
What is the characteristic of the six sense bases?

The differentiation of the faculties constitutes the characteristic of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); because of this, one falls into the sphere of conceptualization and desire (*vitarka-vicāra*).
What is the characteristic of conceptualization and desire?
It is the further arising from the meeting of characteristics; this is the characteristic of conceptualization and desire, because of which one falls into the sphere of sensation (*vedanā*).
What is the characteristic of feeling (*vedanā*)?
Contact and sensation are the characteristic of feeling; from this, one falls into the sphere of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
What is the characteristic of craving?
Setting out [toward an object] is the characteristic of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); by means of this, one is led to fall into the sphere of sensation (*vedanā*).
What is the characteristic of sensation?
Appropriating is the characteristic of sensation; by means of this, one is led to fall into the sphere of existence (*bhava*).
What is the characteristic of existence (*bhava-nimitta*)?
That which causes one to fall into various states is the characteristic of existence; it causes one to descend from here into a place of birth.
What is the characteristic of birth (*jāti-nimitta*)?
The existence of the five aggregates is the characteristic of birth; by means of this, one is led to fall into the state of old age.
What is the characteristic of old age?
Its maturation is the characteristic of old age; by means of this, one is led to fall into the state of death.
What are the signs of death?
The exhaustion of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) constitutes the sign of death; by means of this, one is led to fall into states of suffering.
What are the signs of suffering?
Urgency regarding the body is the characteristic of suffering; it causes one to fall into an undesirable state.
What is the characteristic of the undesirable?
Urgency regarding the mind is the characteristic of the undesirable; it causes one to fall into a state of distress and sorrow.
What is the characteristic of dejection (*upāyāsa*)?
It is to be distressed regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which leads one to fall into a state of sorrow and lamentation.
What is the characteristic of grief and sorrow (*parideva*)?
The voice utters sounds that cause grief and distress; distress becomes grief, and grief likewise becomes distress.
At the nine points of severance, one acts as a companion for all wandering spirits, following along with their flow.
There are two fundamental roots from which offenses arise, namely the three fetters, and there are also the four inversions.
What are the two fundamental roots of those offenses?
The first is delusion (*moha*), and the second is falling into craving for existence (*bhavarāga*); these are called the two fundamental roots.
What are the three roots of defilement?
First is greed, second is hatred, and third is delusion; these are called the three roots of defilement.
There are four inversions; what are the four inversions?
To perceive the impermanent as permanent constitutes an inversion of thought, an inversion of mind, and an inversion of view; this is one inversion.
To reckon suffering as pleasure, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure—these inversions of thought and view are as described above; these are called the four inversions.
That delusion is defined as not understanding the Four Noble Truths:
it is a lack of wisdom, a failure to see, a lack of correspondence, and a failure to understand that feeling constitutes the source of suffering;
this is delusion. What is craving for existence?
To set out toward worldly desires and not relinquish them constitutes craving for existence (*bhavarāga*); this is called the second root.
What is the root of that desire and greed?
It is the greed for whatever place one occupies, for rare treasures, for extraordinary wealth, for exquisite ornaments, and for the envy found therein.
Greed consists of the desire for what is desirable, the aspect of craving, the aspect of longing, and the failure to relinquish; this is the root of the defilement of greed.
Of what is this the root?
It is the root of all greed, of unrighteous conduct of body, unrighteous conduct of speech, and unrighteous conduct of mind, as well as other associated factors.
That which is produced by the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) has mental attention as its root; therefore, it is called the root of the latent tendency of greed.
What is that which is not the root of the unrighteousness of hatred? Is it in a human or in a non-human?

One who harbors the mark of anger and is angry, being intolerant and ignorant, gives rise to resentment and harsh criticism due to the conditions of anger. Thinking what is improper and speaking what is improper, one’s thoughts and speech are unfavorable, causing the mind to recoil; this is the unrighteous root of hatred.
Of what is this the root?

It is not the root of the Dharma; rather, the offenses of body, the offenses of speech, the offenses of mind, and other associated volitions—these are the roots of the Dharma. Therefore, it is anger that is called the root of non-Dharma.
What is that delusion and confusion which is the root of non-Dharma?

It is not knowing the Four Noble Truths as they truly are; it is not understanding, not seeing, not corresponding with, and not comprehending them; it is accepting what is not Dharma, whether by following it or receiving it, whether by abiding in it or failing to recognize it, or being shrouded in the darkness of ignorance within darkness.

It obscures and covers [the mind], causing it to be darkened, causing it to be sightless, and causing wisdom to be destroyed; knowing this, one realizes that it cannot lead to the unconditioned transcendence of the world—this is the root of delusion, non-Dharma, and the snare of craving.
What is this root of delusion and non-Dharma?

It is the performance of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; it is also assisting others in performing what is non-Dharma, and whatever is conceived by the mind as the root of non-Dharma—this is called the root of delusion and non-Dharma.
He should know that; he should know the inversion; he should know that which is inverted; he should know that it arises from that which is inverted.
He possesses one inversion; from one inversion there arise four inversions; from all [of them] there arise three inversions.
What is the single inversion?
It is to perceive or accept that which is impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, non-self as self, and the impure as pure; this is the single inversion.
What are the four inversions?
All [perceptions of] body, sensation, mind, and phenomena constitute the four inversions.
What are the three inversions?
First is perception, second is thought, and third is view; these constitute the three inversions.

When the mind causes the faculty of the eye to become attached to what is agreeable—whether it be form or image—and experiences them through sensation and perception, this is called the perception of desire.
To think that there is the perception of desire, which persists for a long time without ceasing and dwells within mental attention—this is the seed of the thought of desire.
If one discriminates and experiences what has been so perceived, this is called a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).
When that deluded mind does not accord with reality as it perceives, and one fails to understand what should be relinquished, this is called a perversion of the mind (*citta-viparyāsa*).

Because one clings to what should not be clung to, fixating the mindfulness upon form, one reckons the impure mind to be pure; thus, when one hears and assents to these thoughts, and the mind dwells upon the pleasure of what is seen and experienced, this is called a perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
Having seen those [objects], one forms conceptual discriminations based on their marks;
these should be understood as twelve inversions.
What are the twelve? There are three regarding the body, three regarding sensation, three regarding the mind, and three regarding phenomena.
There are four inversions of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), four inversions of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and four inversions of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*);
when these are combined with the meeting of conditions through the entry into form (*rūpa*), they constitute twelve inversions.
The three regarding the body, the three regarding sensation, the three regarding the mind, and the three regarding phenomena combine to form twelve inversions.
These six [sets] constitute seventy-two inversions.
From their original causes and conditions, they arise in accordance with those conditions; they are immeasurable and incalculable, existing in countless people as countless inversions.
Those five aggregates constitute the four bodies: from the existence of the aggregate of form, it belongs to the body;
from the existence of the aggregate of sensation, it belongs to the body of sensation;
from the existence of the aggregate of consciousness, it belongs to the mental body.
From the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and likewise from the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), these belong to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
From the existence of these five aggregates, one causes the four bodies to arise through the conditions of grasping (*upādāna*).
To perceive that body as pure when it is impure is the perversion regarding the body (*kāyaviparyāsa*).
To reckon suffering as pleasure is the perversion regarding suffering;
to reckon the impermanent mind as permanent is the perversion regarding the mind;
to reckon that which is not the self as the self is the perversion regarding phenomena.
In order to rectify the four inversions, the Buddha manifested the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and explained their analytical distinctions.
By contemplating the body as having the characteristics of the body, one attains liberation from the inversion of perceiving the impure as pure;
by contemplating feelings as having the characteristics of feeling, one attains liberation from the inversion of reckoning suffering as pleasure.
He contemplates the mind as the characteristic of the mind and attains liberation from the perversion of regarding what is impermanent as permanent;
he contemplates phenomena as the characteristic of phenomena and attains liberation from the perversion of regarding what is non-self as self.
To be shrouded in darkness within darkness and thus lack understanding is the mark of delusion (*moha*);
to desire to go toward that which causes one to fall into a state of inversion is the mark of craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
and because it causes one to receive form as a body, thereby leading to deception and wonderment, this is the mark of greed (*lobha*).
Causing one to fall into taking what is not given, such that it is contrary to one's wishes, is the mark of hatred (*dveṣa*);
causing one to fall into the state of killing and being unable to comprehend the matter is the mark of delusion (*moha*);
causing one to accept the false and fall into a false state by performing those things that should be rejected and accepting them is the mark of [ignorance].

It causes one to fall into the notion of permanence; it causes one not to know that the body, the physical frame, and objects are merely mutual encounters and associations; it causes one to calculate the notion of pleasure and thereby fall into the station of the body; it causes one to fail to understand the characteristics of dharmas and thus give rise to the notion of a self;

it causes one to fall into the notion that "this is I" or "this is mine," whereby one falls into grasping at the characteristics of form and appearance; it causes one to calculate this as the notion of purity;
and it causes one to fall from this state by failing to restrain the sense bases. These constitute the nine categories.
This has already been analyzed; it has been explained that all unwholesome companions are not to be associated with.
This being concluded, those who are learned will understand it, while those who are not learned will ultimately not understand it;
this is something that the wise can understand, while the unwise will ultimately not understand it.
This demon can be understood; one who does not follow its course cannot understand it.
There are nine points of severance that cause all categories of pure dharmas to fall into aggregation. What are these nine?
First, serenity; second, insight; third, non-greed; fourth, non-ill will; fifth, non-delusion; sixth, impermanence; seventh, suffering; eighth, non-self; ninth, impurity—these are the nine.

That stillness is called *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness). Being able to settle, having settled, correctly settling, gathering in, not losing, being without mental striving, and the mind being tranquil—directing one's attention toward each [object] in this way is what is meant by "stilling."
What is contemplation?

Contemplation is defined as the thorough understanding of the aggregates, the thorough understanding of the bases, the thorough understanding of the sense-spheres, the thorough understanding of names, the thorough understanding of that which arises from the root, the thorough understanding of that which has arisen from the fundamental dharma, the thorough understanding of suffering, the thorough understanding of its origin, the thorough understanding of its cessation, the thorough understanding of the path, the thorough understanding of how things arise from wholesome and unwholesome causes, the thorough understanding of their further increase, the thorough understanding of the white and the black, and the thorough understanding of what is to be followed and what is not to be followed.

If there is such discrimination, whether it be dragging or not dragging, descending or further descending, mindfulness or further mindfulness, reflection, consciousness, wisdom, the eye, deliberation, fulfillment, understanding, insight, clarity, desire, radiance, non-abandonment of courage, contemplation of phenomena, the factors of awakening, right view, or the elements of the Path—this is called contemplation.
Furthermore, there are several pairs of contemplations: first, the contemplation of purity; second, the contemplation of impurity;

third, the contemplation of clarity; fourth, the contemplation of lack of clarity; fifth, the contemplation of black; sixth, the contemplation of white; seventh, the contemplation of what is to be avoided; eighth, the contemplation of what is not to be avoided; ninth, the contemplation of sinful avoidance; tenth, the contemplation of calamity and fortune; eleventh, the contemplation of bondage; twelfth, the contemplation of liberation; thirteenth, the contemplation of that which is beneficial; fourteenth, the contemplation of losing that which is not beneficial; fifteenth, the contemplation of going; sixteenth, the contemplation of returning; seventeenth, the contemplation of receiving retribution for sins; eighteenth, the contemplation of eliminating sins. For this reason, they are called "contemplations."
Furthermore, for two reasons this teaching was established to bring cessation: all people in the world have two kinds of illness.
What are these two? First is delusion; second is craving.
Because there are these two illnesses, the Buddha manifests two medicines.
What are the two? First is cessation (śamatha), and second is insight (vipaśyanā).
If one employs two medicines to cure two diseases, one causes [the practitioner] to realize for themselves:
having abandoned craving and desire, they no longer harbor greedy thoughts and their mind attains liberation; having dispelled delusion, they attain liberation through wisdom.
*Śarīrārthapada-sūtra*, Volume Upper;
*Śarīrārthapada-sūtra*, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
What is that medicine for craving? It is cessation. When craving has ceased, the mind is liberated;
when the mind is liberated, the disease is healed.
What is that medicine for delusion?
This is for the purpose of contemplation. Once delusion has been dispelled, one is liberated through wisdom; this constitutes the healing of the illness.
Thus the Buddha taught: regarding these two phenomena, you should know that the first is name (*nāma*) and the second is form (*rūpa*).
Two things should be abandoned:
first, delusion; second, craving.
Two things should be known for oneself:
The first is wisdom, and the second is liberation.
These two dharmas can be cultivated:
the first is tranquility (śamatha), and the second is insight (vipaśyanā).

Having practiced that tranquility (*śamatha*), he causes consciousness to cognize forms; having cognized them, he causes craving to attain relinquishment (*upekṣā*). Once craving has ceased, the mind becomes liberated, and he realizes this for himself.

Having fulfilled the practice of tranquility, he attains the relinquishment of delusion (*moha*); having attained the relinquishment of delusion, he attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*), and he realizes this for himself.

If a bhikṣu, by means of these two dharmas, personally knows both name and form, and by means of these two dharmas, has abandoned both delusion and craving—then, being thus entirely without attachment, his practice should be considered complete.

If one desires to transcend the world, it means there is still a remnant of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) that has not yet been transcended; once the unconditioned is fully realized and life has reached its ultimate end, suffering is exhausted, ensuring that no further suffering shall arise hereafter.

Because he possesses these aggregates, he both maintains them and enters into them; yet, once they are exhausted and stilled, from that point on there are no more aggregates to maintain or enter. Without further connection, they do not arise again; this is called "without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa).
Having already attained transcendence and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), these two constitute the seeds of the unconditioned.
What is the root of non-attachment and purity?
It is that which, within the three realms, does not grasp, does not hope for, and does not seek; this is called the root of non-attachment and purity.
What is the root of this?
It is non-attachment to the purity of body and the purity of speech;
furthermore, it is the mental attention toward the purity of other associated dharmas that serves as the root, and this is the root of the purity of non-attachment.
There is also the root of purity, which the Buddha has taught as eight kinds of practice; these are the roots of purity.
They constitute the three kinds of pure paths and are the roots of non-attachment.
What are the three?
First is the direct application of skillful means;
second is direct mindfulness.
Third is right concentration.
These are the roots of the three kinds of pure paths; therefore, they are called the root of purity through non-attachment.
What are the roots of non-hatred and non-transgression of the Dharma?

If one endures what provokes anger, then in the future there will be no cause or condition for the arising of anger; by being without anger and not receiving the retribution of anger, one is without malice, without hatred, and does not hate; one is without resentment and does not conceive resentment—this is being without anger and not violating the root of the Dharma.
Therefore, this is called the root of the dharma of non-ill will and non-transgression.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of pure paths:
first, the root of the dharma of non-ill will and non-transgression as right speech; second, as right action; and third, as right livelihood.
These are the three kinds of pure paths; therefore, they are called the root of the dharma of non-ill will and non-transgression.
What is that root of purity which is free from delusion?
It is to see the Four Truths as they truly are through wisdom; to receive purity as it truly is; to be neither ignorant nor deluded; and neither to follow delusion nor to fall into delusion.
The clear manifestation of wisdom is seen through the dharma of purity; this is the root of purity free from delusion.
Of what is this the root?

It is the root of purity free from delusion—the basis for the bodily actions, the verbal expressions, and the mental activities that are likewise connected to the dharma of purity, which are the objects of mental reflection and mindfulness.
Furthermore, they constitute the two seeds of the path to purification for the sake of not being deluded regarding the root:
first, right view; second, right intention.
These are the two seeds of the path to purification that constitute the root.

Therefore, it is called the fundamental purity of non-delusion; this constitutes the three purities and the eightfold path. Having already discerned that all things are impermanent according to their respective conditions, it is thus.
What is that perception of impermanence?
All that is clung to is the perception of impermanence; whatever is perceived and reckoned as known is what constitutes feeling—this is the perception of impermanence.
Furthermore, there are the eight worldly dharmas. What are these eight?
Gain and loss, fame and insignificance, praise and blame, and suffering and pleasure.

To ensure that the mind does not fall into or accept [defilements], and to refrain from accepting various volitions, one practices cessation, protection, and contemplation; when the thought of evil ceases through such practice, this is called the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).
What is that perception of suffering?
It is the perception of suffering that arises from all worldly activities, which is cognized, felt, and experienced; this is called the perception of suffering. From this, what follows?

One regards the perception of suffering as already practiced and increased, with its mental cultivation already extensive; it serves to bring greed to an end, to prevent one from falling into greed, and to ensure that the mind does not receive or fall [into it], remaining unattached and free from recollection.
Having contemplated the guarding of the mind in this way, evil ceases; from this, one reflects upon and attains this essential point.
What is that which is not the perception of a body?
It is when one does not conceive of all phenomena as a body and does not fall into the notion of a body, yet perceives and knows perceptions and feelings; this is called the perception of non-body.

From this, what follows? Having attained the perception of non-self, one applies mindfulness and reflection; having increased this, one causes the self-conception "this is I" to cease. One does not grasp at various mental states, nor does one dwell upon them; through observation, evil and unwholesome states are stilled. This is how one proceeds from these essentials.
What is that perception of foulness?
It is when one perceives all that is loathsome in the world as impure, and having perceived it, knows and experiences it for oneself; this is called the perception of foulness.
From this perception, what is attained?

Having directed one’s attention toward the perception of impurity, through mindfulness, reflection, and further cultivation, one causes the mind to withdraw from and relinquish the five worldly pleasures; it is no longer drawn toward them, does not accept them, and does not fall back into them. By means of various forms of mindfulness, one attains protection, becomes free from evil, and finds firm footing—this is the attainment resulting from this practice.
He practices four applications of mindfulness. Why is this?

It is so that he may know the five aggregates; therefore, the Buddha speaks of these as "discriminations. By means of the perception of impurity, he brings about the liberation of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). By means of the perception of suffering, he brings about the liberation of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). By means of the perception of non-self, he brings about the liberation of the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Through the cultivation of the perception of impermanence, one brings about the liberation of the aggregate of consciousness from it;
through the cultivation of tranquility, one brings about the liberation of craving from it;
through the cultivation of insight, one brings about the liberation of delusion from it.
He practices non-greed in order to abandon greed;
he practices non-ill will in order to abandon ill will;
he practices non-delusion in order to abandon delusion.
From the perception of impermanence, he causes them to understand what is permanent;
from the perception of suffering, he causes them to understand the perception of pleasure;
from the perception of non-self, he causes them to understand the perception of self.
From that perception of impurity, he seeks to resolve the perception of purity.
By means of tranquility (*śamatha*), he is able to withdraw his mind; this is the perception of tranquility, which causes him to enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) through this tranquility.
When one is able to attain understanding and acceptance through the tranquility of all phenomena, this is called "contemplation of perception," which causes one to abide in all-knowingness.
When one is able to attain the cessation of perception from desire, this is called the "mark of non-greed," which causes one to cease taking what is not given.
Thereafter, one no longer gives rise to delusion; this is the absence of the perception of ill-will, which causes one to cease from killing.

To recognize both phenomena and things is the characteristic of non-delusion, which serves to bring about cessation. The cessation of that which is worldly, that which is conditioned, and that which is the characteristic of the phenomena capable of being grasped—this is the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).
One causes them to know that [suffering] arises from this and also knows that it ceases from this;

consciousness is the locus for this. It serves as the bait for the world and acts as the renewal of the world. Whatever is perceived through consciousness is suffering; whatever is conceived through thought is the source of the seeds of pain.
Not dwelling on any phenomena with conceptualization is the non-conceptualization of the body; this is the thought of ideation.
Having seen the corpse of the body already decomposed and bloated blue, to receive this sign is the thought of impurity.
From this point on, one should turn back from remorse and cause it to cease in stillness.
These are the nine stages, which have already been explained in detail.
As for the category of all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) that has been seen, who is it that possesses this complete exposition?
One who knows that much learning or little learning does not constitute wisdom;
because one lacks wisdom, the mind does not remain constantly on the sūtras, but rather the mind becomes linked to the arising of [conceptual] signs.
This occurs because one does not practice non-discriminative contemplation.
They cause one not to attain the perception of impermanence and not to receive the perception of impermanence;
they cause one to fall from this into the five pleasures;
they cause one to be shrouded by the five pleasures and to lose what one ought to strive for.
It causes one not to comprehend the perception of suffering;
it causes one to fall into the appropriation of the five aggregates;
and it causes one to mentally conceive of this as a self.

One does not view the various parts as a single entity, yet one does not abandon them nor contemplate them in such a way as to fall into the notion that they are not the body, for the mind remains fixed upon their appearance.

One delights in calculating this body as pure, rather than calculating it as being covered by skin and muscle, so as not to fall into the notion of impurity; thus one does not abide in sensation or cessation.
This means that by not believing in perceptions, one causes perceptions to cease to exist and does not experience joy.
Having abandoned these four kinds [of perceptions], one falls into the state of the unconditioned realm.

The Buddha taught the faculty of faith: if a bhikṣu wishes to see and know it, he should seek it within the four *śrotāpatti-aṅgas* as the pure dharmas; without relinquishing the characteristics of skillful means, he brings about purification, and from that purity, he initiates the practice so as to fall into the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The Buddha taught the faculty of diligence; if a bhikṣu wishes to see and know it, he should abide in the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Whatever has been experienced in the past, if one recollects it with mindfulness without forgetting, this non-forgetfulness gives rise to the falling [into] the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu wishes to see and know the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya), he should contemplate it as being present in the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni).
By forming a single-pointed mental focus, this constitutes concentration arising from non-delusion, which causes one to enter the stages of the four dhyānas."

The Buddha said: "If one wishes to know the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*) of this bhikṣu, one should know it resides in the four dhyānas; calculating from its basis, it constitutes wisdom (*prajñā*). If there is one capable of maintaining it, it is from this that it is initiated, causing [the mind] to descend into the Four Noble Truths."
The Buddha taught that if a bhikṣu desires to see the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya), he should abide in the Four Noble Truths.
There are four wheels:
the wheel of dwelling in a favorable district, the wheel of relying on wise people, the wheel of one’s own original right vow, and the wheel of merit from past lives.

That constitutes the characteristic of dwelling together in virtue and the Way; this is what it means to dwell in a favorable district and county, enabling one to find a place where the worthy may take refuge. By attaining the characteristic of relying upon virtue and the Way, this is what it means to rely upon a person of wisdom.

From this, one falls into the state of having right aspirations; by attaining the characteristics of right aspiration, this constitutes the right aspiration of the body, which causes one to fall into the realm of merit.
From the characteristics of entry arising from pure conduct, this is called merit, which leads one to fall into the realm of the five pleasures.
That constitutes the eleven fundamentals of the Dharma of precepts: first, one maintains the precepts for the sake of freedom from remorse regarding form;

second, for the sake of attaining a joyful mind through being without remorse; third, for the sake of generating affection through having a joyful mind; fourth, for the sake of attaining tranquility of the body through having affection of the mind; fifth, for the sake of attaining pleasure through having tranquility of the body; sixth, for the sake of attaining right stillness through having pleasure of the mind; seventh, for the sake of knowing things as they truly are through having right stillness of the mind; eighth, for the sake of becoming tranquil through knowing things as they truly are; ninth, for the sake of attaining detachment through being tranquil; tenth, for the sake of attaining liberation through attaining detachment; eleventh, for the sake of seeing with wisdom through attaining liberation.
Possessing wisdom, one knows that birth and death have been exhausted, the path has been traversed, what was to be done has been accomplished, and one will no longer return to undergo suffering.
What are the characteristics of this precept?
Maintaining the precepts until the end of life causes one to reach a state free from regret.
When the body does not increase the signs of transgression, this constitutes being without regret; from this, one reaches joy and attains a state of happiness.
The aspect of being agreeable is joy (*muditā*), which leads to the state of endearment.
The aspect of contentment is the basis (*sthiti*), which leads to the state of reliance (*praśrabdhi*).
From that reliance arises the aspect of attainment, which leads to the state of bliss (*sukha*).
Having already eliminated covetousness as the mark of pleasure, one causes oneself to attain the state of concentration.
When the mind follows its tendencies without forgetfulness, this constitutes the mark of concentration; it causes one to reach the state of wisdom as it truly is, free from delusion.
When the characteristic of reality follows the characteristic of conformity, this is the state of tranquility.
If one knows that what is not the body is the mark of tranquility, one causes it to lead from this to the state of separation from marks.
Not approaching or associating with them constitutes separation from marks; by means of this, one attains liberation.
Having already acted contrary to the Dharma, one does not suffer its retribution; this is the mark of liberation, which brings about the wisdom and vision of liberation.
There are four stages of the path to virtue; what are these four?
It is the merit of one who practices the four foundations of mindfulness. If he possesses such knowledge and wisdom, this constitutes the stage of vision;
it is the merit of attaining the path, which is the attainment of the traces of the path.
When one knows existence as it truly is and thus rejects and distances oneself from it, this is called the Stage of Thinning (*tanubhūmi*); it is the merit of those who go and return.
When one regards that which has been rejected as useless and thereby distances oneself from it, this is called the Stage of Complete Separation (*vītarāgabhūmi*);
having already become separated, this is the merit of non-returning, called the Stage of the End of Desire, where there is no further attachment.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "the merit of one who has entered the stream" (*sotāpanna*)?
A disciple of the Way possesses eight factors of the path; therefore, they are called "one who has entered the stream.
This is their merit; for this reason, it is called "the merit of one who has entered the stream."
Why is this? Because it is called "purity" by virtue of being pure; this constitutes pure merit and this constitutes the Way and its Virtue.
There are eight kinds of paths of purity that constitute this merit; therefore, it is called "pure merit."

Regarding that which one ought to attain as the path to the tracks (sotāpatti): how is it that the disciple, through the path associated with the truths already realized, severs the three fetters? What are those three fetters?
First, to know that the body is not the self; second, to be free from doubt; third, not to trade or barter the precepts.

Having severed these three fetters, the disciple of the Way enters the stream of the Path (srotāpanna); they no longer fall into the evil realms, and having at most undergone seven more births among the heavens and likewise among humans, wherever they go and come, suffering is cut off. Having attained liberation from suffering, this is called the "ground of vision" (*darśana-bhūmi*), and it constitutes the merit of attaining the stream-entry.
What is it that causes the mind to descend into this body and also come to know this body?

It is because of delusion, because of not having heard [the teaching], because one is a worldly person who has neither seen nor awakened to the Awakened One, nor has one followed those who have heard, received the precepts, or heard the teachings, and furthermore, because one has not yet made such distinctions.
Manifesting the True Dharma as mental activity, this form is the body.
Surveying all forms as the body, this form is also the body; form is also my own body. Feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness are also as explained above.

Having thus attained this contemplation, one then experiences the five pleasures, causing oneself to accept this body and fall into attachment to the body. One causes the mind to think, "This is I," and "I am defined by this," becoming bound and lacking self-mastery. Being dragged along by these associations, one endures such things; whatever the mind intends to accept, once accepted, it follows after and clings to them. This is false view, which leads to falling into the acceptance of this body.
He views these five perversions, which cause one to fall into the state of non-existence through doubt. What are the five?
If one views form as a self, and likewise views feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as a self—these are the five perverse views that cause one to fall into non-existence.
Thereafter, there are fifteen remaining [views] that cause one to fall into the view of permanence (*śāśvata*).
When one sees that this body has been thus severed, then the sixty-two wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are abandoned;
one does not fall into either permanence or impermanence (*aśāśvata*).
Having abandoned both the impermanent and the permanent, the disciples of the Way are free from inverted false views; they do so solely for the sake of transcending the world.
What is meant by "direct vision"? It is that which prevents one from falling into a body characterized by false views.

If a disciple of the Way has heard [the teaching], possesses direct insight, and has attained penetration through the scriptures, he has already received the crossing over to the unconditioned (*asamskrta*);
he has already understood the dharma of crossing over and no longer views form as the body, but perceives everywhere that form is the body.
This form is also the body’s form, and form is also my own body; when feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are no longer seen, one thus understands the three fetters.
What are these three?
First, not seeing this body; second, being without anger; third, being without doubt.

Having become thus, the disciple of the Way is without doubt regarding the Buddha and has no further doubts. He becomes one of faith, joy, and devotion to the Buddha—namely, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. His wisdom and practice are already complete for the sake of bliss; he is liberated from the world, free from fault, and is a master who tames the Dharma through the Dharma. He teaches the world of gods and men, and as a Buddha, he is supreme.
This is to attain faith and be free from doubt; it is to follow this Dharma, to abide in the Dharma without fetters or doubt, and to possess faith and joy.
When the Buddha teaches this Dharma, it is something that can be studied and realized in the present, something that one personally witnesses now, and its understanding constitutes wisdom.
Having severed the proximity of this craving and thirst, and having followed their severance, there is emptiness with nothing further to be attained.
Love has been destroyed, abandoned, and exhausted; it is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is the second:

being without fetters and without doubt, one attains the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; for the sake of the assembly of fellow students, being without fetters and without doubt, there is already acceptance and joy.
Thus, those disciples who have received the Path constitute the assembly of learners; they receive the training as it should be received.

Their precepts are established, their concentration is settled, and they have attained wisdom and liberation. Having achieved the wisdom of liberation, they have manifested and realized it; these are the disciples of the Buddha who train.
When these four groups are combined, they form eight pairs; this is called the "Eightfold Path of the Sages.

They are held in high esteem and honored by the world, being peerless, worthy of offerings, service, and reverence. They are a field of merit beyond compare, served both by devas and humans; this is the third [type of person].
Having become free from doubt regarding the Dharma, one follows the Dharma; all that is followed is suffering.
Having become free from the fetter of doubt, having already received and rejoiced, it arises with craving as its condition; suffering likewise arises with craving as its condition.
When doubt and fetters have ceased, when what was received has been understood, and when delight and craving have been exhausted, this is the end of suffering.
Thus, being without doubt and without fetters, having attained this reception, one attains the exhaustion of delight and craving; this is the end of suffering.
Regarding the fetter of doubt: once it is resolved, one receives joy and this constitutes the eighth limb of the Path.
From this reception of the limbs, one brings about the exhaustion of suffering; thus, one no longer doubts. Being without doubt, one is no longer fettered; falling into liberation, one attains joy.
If there are originally doubts that cannot be resolved—whether regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha;

or if there are originally doubts regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path—then one is deluded by these matters and fails to understand them, following after whatever the mind suspects and doubts.
In this regard, what is this "sore"?

It is that which has already been understood and its root already severed; the tree no longer remains, having been dispersed it does not reappear, and the original dharma from whence it came does not arise again.
That one who maintains the *śīla* of abstinence (*brahmacarya*) transforms and exchanges it for two things:
first, falling into craving; second, failing to understand how to avoid [such states].

By maintaining the *śīla* of abstinence and transforming it through such mental orientation, one is governed by this very *śīla*; from this, one shall attain the state of a deva or a companion of devas, and shall dwell in the heavens. There, he is named "Armor," and a jade maiden shall dwell with him, sharing mutual pleasure.
To have such expectations, such desires, and such thoughts, forming attachments and intentions—this is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Although one may observe the precepts of a forest-dweller (*āraṇyaka*), if one falls into such deceptive trading, that person does not truly understand the observance of the forest-dweller's precepts.
What is the exchange of conduct?
It is the transgression of the precepts that constitutes the exchange of conduct. What is the transgression of the precepts?

If one thinks that the mind-born being attains purity through precepts, attains liberation through precepts, attains the essential through precepts, or crosses over suffering and pleasure through them; or if one thinks that the mind-born being crosses over through vows—this is called failing to understand the upholding of the *śīla* (precepts) and instead engaging in exchange and bartering.
For what reason is it called "unresolved imitation"?

It arises from clothing and from vows that lead to transcendence; it arises from the departure from suffering and pleasure. Thus, these two types of karma—clothing and vows—are what constitute "imitation."
What is meant by "grasping"?

It refers to the aspiration for the two types of precepts and robes, calculating in one's mind that through these one will attain liberation, through these one will attain the essential, through these one will transcend suffering and pleasure, and through these sufferings and pleasures one will attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

From this, there is incorrect reckoning of the Dharma; one is not liberated by this, yet the mind reckons that liberation comes from this. Taking what is incorrect to be correct, one follows this craving and exists in such a way, with acceptance, expectation, fetters, and views. To think that liberation comes from this is non-liberation; to maintain precepts while engaging in trade and exchange is the second fetter.
The disciples who have attained the Way have already relinquished [defilements]; as they are without root, they have been severed.
The tree has been uprooted and no longer appears; it will not grow again hereafter. This Dharma is thus completely purified.
Precepts such as those for attaining the Path—following them without breaking, piercing, losing, or regretting them;
merely increasing in accordance with them, being acceptable to the wise, and being incapable of being taken away; by means of this one attains concentration. These constitute the three fetters.

The disciple on the path has already severed [the fetters], having entered the track of the Way; he will no longer fall into unwholesome states and is certain to transcend the world, passing through seven more births among devas and humans.
Once the period of these births and deaths is completed, he shall attain the essential liberation from suffering.
There are four kinds of association. What are the four kinds of association?
First, association through understanding; second, association through abandonment and relinquishment; third, association through personal realization; and fourth, association through fulfillment.
That disciple of the Dharma and Vinaya corresponds with the realization that suffering has been understood;
corresponds with the relinquishing of the abandonment of its origin;
and corresponds with the personal realization of its cessation.
From the perspective of the Path, this constitutes the correspondence of fulfillment.
It consists of the concurrent practice of tranquility and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), occurring in a single location, at one time, and with a single intention.
Originally, there exists this mental faculty (*manas*), which is made to perform four functions.
What are the four? First is suffering (*duḥkha*); having been liberated from suffering, it is associated with suffering.
Second is the origin (*samudaya*); having been abandoned through the cutting off of the origin, it is associated with the origin.
Third is cessation (*nirodha*); through the direct realization of cessation, one becomes associated with cessation.
Fourth is the path (*mārga*); through the fulfillment of the path, one becomes associated with the path.
Why is it that, having already been liberated from suffering, one is associated [with the path]?
For what reason is there correspondence with the abandonment through the cultivation [of the path]?
For what reason is there correspondence with the personal realization through the exhaustion [of defilements]?
For what reason is there correspondence with the increase and fulfillment through the path?
There is an analogy for this:
it is like a mass of foam on water that moves along until it reaches the far shore; there are four crocodiles there.
From this bank, it proceeds to cross to the other bank; having crossed and reached the shore, its continuity is severed.
It is also like this: when śamatha and vipaśyanā are practiced together, in one place, at one time, and with one intention, they reach the ultimate goal to accomplish four matters.
For example, when the sun rises and reaches its zenith, it performs four functions:
bringing forth light, destroying darkness, manifesting forms, and reaching its culmination.
It is like a boat crossing over: leaving this shore, reaching the far shore, carrying the cargo, and cutting the mooring rope.

Insight and tranquility (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) are also like this; they proceed as a pair, functioning in a single location, at one time, and with a single intention. Their ultimate goal is to accomplish four tasks:

to illuminate suffering according to its true characteristics, to sever the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) through their appropriate application, to realize the exhaustion [of outflows] through appropriate liberation, and to cultivate the essential path through appropriate application.
Why is this? Because suffering is associated with the analytical knowledge of contact;
accumulation is associated with the analytical knowledge of abandonment.

The cessation of suffering is associated with the realization of liberation; the path is associated with the essential realization of liberation. *Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are likewise: they proceed in tandem, in a single place, at one time, and with a single mind. One must bring *śamatha* to its ultimate conclusion, which constitutes the fourth of the four matters to be perfected: [1] The perfection of the basis (*āśraya-pariniṣpatti*); [2] The perfection of the object (*ālambana-pariniṣpatti*); [3] The perfection of the application (*prayoga-pariniṣpatti*); [4] The perfection of the fruit (*phala-pariniṣpatti*). Regarding these: [1] The perfection of the basis refers to the body being free from illness and the mind being free from affliction. [2] The perfection of the object refers to the objects of meditation being pure and the mental states being clear. [3] The perfection of the application refers to the correct practice of the means of accomplishment. [4] The perfection of the fruit refers to the attainment of the fruit of the path through the cultivation of the path. Furthermore, there are four kinds of perfection: [1] Perfection of the cause (*hetu-pariniṣpatti*); [2] Perfection of the condition (*pratyaya-pariniṣpatti*); [3] Perfection of the fruit (*phala-pariniṣpatti*); [4] Perfection of the function (*karma-pariniṣpatti*). Regarding these: [1] The perfection of the cause refers to the causes for attaining the fruit of the path, such as the roots of goodness and the seeds of liberation. [2] The perfection of the condition refers to the conditions for attaining the fruit of the path, such as the teachings of a Buddha and the instruction of a spiritual friend. [3] The perfection of the fruit refers to the actualization of the fruit of the path, such as the various stages of sainthood. [4] The perfection of the function refers to the functions performed by the fruit of the path, such as the benefit of self and others. Moreover, there are four kinds of perfection: [1] Perfection of the stage (*bhūmi-pariniṣpatti*); [2] Perfection of the practice (*caryā-pariniṣpatti*); [3] Perfection of the power (*bala-pariniṣpatti*); [4] Perfection of the wisdom (*jñāna-pariniṣpatti*). Regarding these: [1] The perfection of the stage refers to the various stages of the bodhisattva path, such as the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). [2] The perfection of the practice refers to the practices of the bodhisattvas, such as the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). [3] The perfection of the power refers to the powers of the bodhisattvas, such as the ten powers (*daśabala*). [4] The perfection of the wisdom refers to the wisdoms of the bodhisattvas, such as the four types of analytical knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*). Furthermore, there are four kinds of perfection: [1] Perfection of the initial entry (*praveśa-pariniṣpatti*); [2] Perfection of the abiding (*sthiti-pariniṣpatti*); [3] Perfection of the emergence (*niṣkramaṇa-pariniṣpatti*); [4] Perfection of the ultimate goal (*niṣṭhā-pariniṣpatti*). Regarding these: [1] The perfection of the initial entry refers to the initial entry into the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). [2] The perfection of the abiding refers to the abiding in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). [3] The perfection of the emergence refers to the emergence from the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). [4] The perfection of the ultimate goal refers to the finality of the path, which is the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Furthermore, there are four kinds of perfection: [1] Perfection of the self-nature (*svabhāva-pariniṣpatti*); [2] Perfection of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pariniṣpatti*); [3] Perfection of the differentiation (*prabheda-pariniṣpatti*); [4] Perfection of the synthesis (*samuccaya-pariniṣpatti*). Regarding these: [1] The perfection of the self-nature refers to the true nature of all phenomena, which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). [2] The perfection of the characteristics refers to the characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned. [3] The perfection of the differentiation refers to the distinctions between the various vehicles (*yāna*) and the various levels of attainment. [4] The perfection of the synthesis refers to the convergence of all wholesome dharmas into the single vehicle (*ekayāna*). Furthermore, there are four kinds of perfection: [1] Perfection of the mundane (*laukika-pariniṣpatti*); [2] Perfection of the supramundane (*lokottara-pariniṣpatti*); [3] Perfection of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-pariniṣpatti*); [4] Perfection of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-pariniṣpatti*). Regarding these: [1] The perfection of the mundane refers to the worldly attainments, such as the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). [2] The perfection of the supramundane refers to the transcendental attainments, such as the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*). [3] The perfection of the conditioned refers to the fruits of the path that arise from effort. [4] The perfection of the unconditioned refers to the fruit of the path that is beyond effort and conceptualization. Furthermore, there are four kinds of perfection: [1] Perfection of the provisional (*neyārtha-pariniṣpatti*); [2] Perfection of the definitive (*nītārtha-pariniṣpatti*); [3] Perfection of the teaching (*deśanā-pariniṣpatti*); [4] Perfection of the realization (*adhigama-pariniṣpatti*). Regarding these: [1] The perfection of the provisional refers to the teachings that require further interpretation. [2] The perfection of the definitive refers to the teachings that reveal the ultimate truth. [3] The perfection of the teaching refers to the verbal expression of the Dharma. [4] The perfection of the realization refers to the internal experience of the Dharma. Furthermore, there are four kinds of perfection: [1] Perfection of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-pariniṣpatti*); [2] Perfection of the abandonment (*prahāṇa-pariniṣpatti*); [3] Perfection of the transformation (*parāvṛtti-pariniṣpatti*); [4] Perfection of the mastery (*vaśitā-pariniṣpatti*). Regarding these: [1] The perfection of the antidote refers to the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣikā dharmāḥ*). [2] The perfection of the abandonment refers to the eradication of the afflictions (*kleśa*). [3] The perfection of the transformation refers to the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). [4] The perfection of the mastery refers to the attainment of the ten masteries (*daśavaśitā*). Furthermore, there are four kinds of perfection: [1] Perfection of the accumulation (*saṃbhāra-pariniṣpatti*); [2] Perfection of the path (*mārga-pariniṣpatti*); [3] Perfection of the fruit (*phala-pariniṣpatti*); [4] Perfection of the activity (*karman-pariniṣpatti*). Regarding these: [1] The perfection of the accumulation refers to the two accumulations of merit and wisdom. [2] The perfection of the path refers to the five paths of the bodhisattva.
