It is for the full understanding of suffering, for the abandonment of its origin, for the realization of its cessation, and for the fulfillment of the path.
It is like lighting a lamp: it performs four functions from beginning to end—it provides illumination, dispels darkness, reveals forms, and removes doubt.
Śamatha and vipaśyanā are likewise; they perform four tasks:
to recognize suffering, to sever its origin, to realize its cessation for oneself, and to fulfill the path.
This is like lighting a lamp that burns until the end, which possesses four meanings:
To manifest light, to dispel darkness, to reveal forms, and to exhaust the oil and the wick—so too it is with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Practiced together as a pair, reaching their ultimate consummation in a single place, at one time, and with a single mind, they perform four functions:

to recognize suffering through its association with suffering; to sever the tendencies through their association with the tendencies; to realize the exhaustion [of outflows] through its association with the realization of exhaustion; and to cultivate the path through its association with the fullness of the path.
For what reason is it associated with the suffering of suffering?
For what reason is it associated with the origin of the origin?
For what reason is it associated with the realization of the cessation of cessation through personal realization?
Why is it that one is said to be "in harmony with the path of the seeker and the path of the adept"?
To whom does this correspondence apply? It applies to one who has attained tranquility and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
What is the application?
How should it be maintained? It is the binding of the mind in contemplation.

Having bound the mind in contemplation, one then perceives the suffering of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); that which the mind is bound to is "stopping" (*śamatha*), and having perceived the five aggregates as suffering is "insight" (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding those five aggregates with which one is closely associated—those which could give rise to desire, attachment, and the wish to go toward them and not abandon their habitual practice—these have now been severed and exhausted.

The path of śamatha and vipaśyanā is also like this: it causes these virtues—the Four Noble Truths—to reach their ultimate consummation in a single place, at a single time, and with a single intention, so that the Four Truths may be brought into correspondence.
Such is the Path. For the disciple of the Dharma, this is the characteristic of the Dharma;

having thus attained what is called the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*), and having already acquired the stream of the Path and reached the station of the tracks of the Path, he further practices tranquility and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) so that the fetters of the underlying tendencies of desire and ill-will may be eliminated.

The disciple who has attained the Path undergoes the cycle of coming and going; by this, their footing is established. Having followed through with coming and going, they then destroy the root of suffering; this is the stage of "Thinning" (tanutva-bhūmi).
They have then completed the merit of coming and going and have already arrived at dwelling in virtue.

Furthermore, they increase their tranquility and insight, causing the remaining fetters of craving and aversion to be fully relinquished. While craving and aversion have not yet been fully relinquished, they cause those bonds to be brought to completion. Having thus attained the state of a disciple on the Path, they have already resolved and completed the five lower fetters.

What are these five? First, seeing the faults of the body; second, resolving doubts; third, being neither confused nor wavering in one's precepts; fourth, having no expectations; and fifth, having no resentment—these are the five fetters.

Having completed this, one becomes a disciple who has attained the Way and no longer returns to the world; having crossed over to the beyond, they do not return to this world again. This is called "retreating from the ground," and this is the merit of non-returning.

Having already attained the merit of cessation and non-returning, one further augments the wings of tranquility and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), causing them to effect the abandonment of the five higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*). What are these five?
First, desire for the realm of form (*rūparāga*); second, desire for the formless realm (*arūpyarāga*); third, ignorance (*moha*); fourth, pride (*māna*); and fifth, lack of understanding (*avidyā*).

Having completed these five stages, one has abandoned the five fetters; being thus without attachment, one has crossed over the world and is free from outflows. Having reached the end, one attains liberation through the right path; this is called the completion of the ground.

Even for one who is free from attachment, there still exists the sublime unconditioned; having completed this relinquishment, the life-faculty of the world is exhausted, and the suffering of the world is also exhausted, such that suffering shall not arise again.

Having realized that these aggregates, elements, and sense bases have already ceased and are tranquil, that there are no longer any aggregates, elements, or sense bases, and that they are no longer linked nor will they arise again—this is called the completion of the unconditioned.

For them, he has already taught the application to the Truths; he has also taught the application to the factors, as well as the stages, merit, and abandonment; he has taught transgression and renunciation, and the two unconditioned states—for all such things, he has thus taught.
The Buddha has already completed his further crossing over of the world; if a person wishes to cross over the world, they should follow his example.
What are the nine successive stages of right concentration?

They are the four dhyānas, as well as the four formless right concentrations, and the concentration of the cessation of perception and feeling—these constitute the nine successive stages of right concentration.
In that first dhyāna, five factors have been abandoned, and five factors are present accordingly.
Which five factors have been abandoned?
They are the five hindrances:
First, sensual desire; second, ill will; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; fifth, doubt. These are the five kinds.
The higher dhyānas have already been abandoned.
What is the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*)?

"Sensual desire" refers to that which is pursued: attachment to the five types of pleasure, setting out toward what is sought, and following one's wishes to initiate and give rise to [craving] without relinquishing it; this is called the hindrance of sensual desire.
What is this hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*)?

When a person, having undertaken the practice of cultivation, is driven by the characteristic of resentment and the root of unrighteousness, and from which it arises—this is called the hindrance of ill-will.
What is that hindrance of torpor and drowsiness? Torpor is a settling of the body or a settling of the mind;

it is a stopping of the body or a stopping of the mind; it is a delusion of the body or a delusion of the mind; it is a heaviness of the body or a heaviness of the mind; it is an unfitness of the body or an unfitness of the mind; it is a lack of control over the body or a lack of control over the mind—this is called torpor.
What is torpor (*styāna*)?
It is a state of the mind characterized by dullness; it causes movement to move toward dullness and prevents one from performing tasks—this is torpor.
The former is drowsiness (*middha*), and the latter is torpor; together they are called the hindrance of drowsiness-and-torpor (*middha-styāna-nīvaraṇa*).
What is that which he does not understand regarding the hindrance of remorse?
It is the lack of bodily restraint. What is remorse?

When one reflects upon what is desirable or undesirable and fails to attain freedom from regret—this initial failure to understand leads subsequently to regret; these together are termed the hindrance of remorse due to lack of understanding (*kaukṛtya-āvaraṇa*).
What is this hindrance of doubt?

It refers to those who do not have faith in the Buddha, do not have faith in the Dharma, and do not have faith in the Saṃgha; who do not understand suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; and from whom the fetters and latent tendencies also arise—this is called the hindrance of doubt.
There are also five kinds of doubt:

doubt regarding inhabited settlements, doubt regarding the proclamation of the teaching, doubt regarding the discernment of the path, doubt regarding the attainment of meditative concentration, and doubt regarding the merit of attaining the path.
Thus, this is called the explanation of fixed doubt; these are the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
What is meant by the term "hindrance"?
A hindrance is an obstruction; it is that which obstructs all pure dharmas (*viśuddhadharma*).

What is their antidote? Desire is countered by purity; hatred is countered by equanimity; sleep is countered by stillness; drowsiness is countered by diligence; the five pleasures are countered by joy and stillness; fetters are countered by non-regret; doubt is countered by wisdom; and ignorance regarding the origin of things is countered by clear understanding.

The Buddha’s Explanation of the One Hundred and Sixty-three Samādhis of the Seal of Wisdom. It should be known, Śāriputra!

The body of the Tathāgata is a non-body; it is without action, without arising, without cessation, not derived from existence, never created, without conjunction, without wandering, without arrival, without cognition, without habituation, entirely pure, without accumulation, without aversion, without movement, without stopping, without birth, without retribution, without seeing, without interval, without odor, without taste, without touch, without consciousness, without illumination, without analogy, without cognitive patience, without aspiration, and without thought.
It is not the mind, it is free from the mind; the mind is equanimous yet without equanimity;

it is the departure of the mind. It has nothing with which to associate; the five paths of existence are severed and their essential fetters are fully exhausted. It is without confinement, without affliction, without existence, and without fear. It is neither "is" nor "is not"; it is without karma, without accomplishment, without speech, and without manifestation as either soft or otherwise.
It is neither light nor darkness; neither extinguished nor non-extinguished; having transcended extinction, it is already extinguished;

it is pure, supremely pure. That purity is not employed; it is not delight, not craving, not burdened; having abandoned the burden, it dwells in the state of no-locus. It does not go, does not perish, does not vanish; it is not a dharma, nor is it a non-dharma; it is not a realm, nor is it a non-realm; it is not exhaustion, yet there is no exhaustion; having relinquished exhaustion, it is without anger. It is detached from the heavens, detached from direction, detached from speech, and detached from thought.
Neither conjoined nor disjoined, neither extreme nor non-extreme, neither departing nor not departing, neither dual nor non-delightful.
Without that sensation, without what is viewed, without marks, detached from marks, and not seeking marks—luminous, tranquil and steady, unattached, and detached from attachment—one cultivates faith.

Furthermore, there is no duality of designation; it is as it truly is, thoroughly examined as it truly is. It does not fail those in accordance with its meaning; it is a crossing over where there is nothing to cross over, an elimination where there is nothing to eliminate, a salvation where there is nothing to save, and a teaching where there is nothing to teach. It is equal to non-duality, equal to the peerless, equal to emptiness, equal to the placeless, equal to the unarisen, and equal to the unattainable.

Without rest and free from breath, already stilled and utterly tranquil, fully pacified, liberated, and with the mind’s wholesome conduct turned toward the essential, all retribution is severed; he perfects the exceedingly true body, its luminous substance pure.

It is without self-reflection and without activity; its practice and understanding are without liberation and without response. It is not level, not long, not round, and not square. It does not praise the aggregates (*skandha*), does not extol the elements (*dhātu*), and does not laud the sense bases (*āyatana*). It is not a numerical category, nor can it be brought into enumeration; it is not subject to rebirth, is invisible, possesses no cognition, and yet does not die.

There is no cause that is not a cause for the peerless; the body is thus without falling, and there is no place of abiding. It is neither end nor beginning, neither thought nor anxiety, neither activity nor contention, neither evil appearance nor parinirvāṇa, neither cessation nor completion, neither that which is created nor that which does not wander.
